nameStory: This tiny spider gets its scientific name from Carl Ludwig Walckenaer, a French civil engineer who became fascinated with spiders and wrote groundbreaking works on arachnology in the early 1800s. The species name 'communis' means 'common' in Latin, though ironically this little spider has only been recorded once in New England, making it anything but common in our region!
description: The Common Walckenaeria is a minuscule member of the sheetweb and dwarf weaver family, so small you might mistake it for a speck of dirt at first glance. These tiny spiders are typically dark brown to blackish in color with a glossy appearance. Like other dwarf spiders, they're incredibly small - usually measuring less than 3mm in body length, about the size of a pinhead.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely tiny, less than 3mm long - smaller than most ants and easily overlooked as debris

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with a relatively large cephalothorax (front section) that feels firm when gently touched

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates delicate sheet webs close to the ground that feel silky-smooth and may shimmer with morning dew

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish coloration with a glossy, almost mirror-like sheen on the carapace

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight tiny eyes arranged in two rows, barely visible without magnification but create tiny dark spots

habitat: Look for this elusive spider in leaf litter and low vegetation where it constructs its sheet webs near ground level. Given its extreme rarity in New England, it likely prefers undisturbed forest floors with rich organic matter. The single New England observation suggests it favors specific microhabitats that remain largely unknown.

seasonality.spring: Adults may become active as temperatures warm, though their tiny size makes detection extremely difficult during this period.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found, though still extraordinarily rare in our region.
seasonality.fall: May continue activity into early fall before seeking overwintering sites in leaf litter and soil crevices.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as juveniles or adults hidden deep in leaf litter, completely dormant and invisible.

funFact: Despite being called the 'Common' Walckenaeria, this species has been documented only once in all of New England, making it one of our rarest spiders - you're more likely to find a four-leaf clover than spot one of these tiny arachnids!
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from other dwarf spiders without microscopic examination. The entire family looks like moving specks of dirt to the naked eye, so any tiny dark spider in leaf litter could potentially be this species.
contextualKnowledge: The ironic naming of this species highlights how scientific names don't always reflect local abundance - 'communis' suggests it's common somewhere, but clearly not in New England where it's exceptionally rare.
compareHints: Distinguishing this species from its Walckenaeria relatives like the Spiraling Sheet-web Weaver requires expert examination of reproductive structures under a microscope. All members of this genus are incredibly small, dark-colored dwarf spiders that create sheet webs, making field identification to species level nearly impossible for most observers.
